questions.priority: Know the role of anti-TNF agents in Crohn disease.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for four clients with Crohn disease. Which client should the nurse see first?
options: A client in remission asking about anti-TNF injections
A client with a new fever and dry mucous membranes after many loose stools
A client asking for ideas for a high-protein, low-residue diet
A client with mild diarrhea controlled with loperamide
rationales: A medication question can wait.
The book's nursing priorities are monitoring for infection and dehydration; this client shows signs of both.
Diet teaching is important but not urgent.
Controlled mild diarrhea is stable.
questions.clue: Fever plus signs of dehydration.
questions.priority: Prioritize possible infection and dehydration.

questions.stem: A client newly diagnosed with Crohn disease asks what causes it. Which factors should the nurse include as possible contributors? Select all that apply.
options: Genetic predisposition
Emotional stress as the main cause
Smoking
An overactive proinflammatory immune response
Infectious triggers
rationales: Genetic predisposition is a listed cause.
The book says emotional stress is a result, not a cause.
Smoking is a listed environmental factor.
Immune imbalance with an overactive proinflammatory response is a listed cause.
Infectious agents are listed triggers.
questions.clue: Causes listed in the Crohn disease box.
questions.priority: Teach the factors linked to Crohn disease.

questions.stem: A client in a severe flare of ulcerative colitis is scheduled for a barium enema with air contrast. What should the nurse do?
options: Cancel the test and document the reason.
Tell the client the test carries no risk.
Proceed as scheduled, since the test shows disease distribution.
Hold proceeding and clarify the perforation risk with the provider
rationales: Incorrect. The nurse should hold proceeding for safety and promptly clarify the order rather than independently cancel the diagnostic plan.
Incorrect. Colonic distention in severe active colitis can cause perforation and worsen risk in toxic megacolon.
Incorrect. Do not proceed without resolving the unsafe order.
Correct. Escalate the risk and clarify appropriate imaging or limited endoscopic evaluation according to the clinical condition. A barium enema does not establish histologic disease depth.
questions.clue: Barium enema planned during a severe flare.
questions.priority: Question a test that needs caution in severe disease.
questions.takeaway: Hold and clarify potentially unsafe colonic distention during severe colitis; use the team's safer diagnostic plan.

questions.stem: The nurse is taking the health history of a client with ulcerative colitis. Which findings are associated with the disease and should be included in the history? Select all that apply.
options: Low-grade fevers
Joint swelling
Right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals
Eye inflammation such as uveitis
Pain that worsens after a bowel movement
rationales: The book says to ask about low-grade fevers.
Joint swelling is an inflammatory condition the book says to ask about.
Right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals suggests gallbladder disease, not ulcerative colitis.
Uveitis is an inflammatory condition the book says to ask about.
In ulcerative colitis, abdominal pain is relieved by defecation, so pain that worsens afterward is not typical.
questions.clue: Fevers and other inflammatory conditions.
questions.priority: Assess for related inflammatory findings in ulcerative colitis.

questions.stem: A client with ulcerative colitis has 15 bloody stools a day, dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor and weakness. Which nursing action best protects the client's safety?
options: Encourage the client to walk to the bathroom alone to keep up strength.
Allow independent toileting as long as the client feels steady sitting up.
Limit fluids to reduce the number of stools.
Provide a bedside commode or help with toileting, using fall precautions.
rationales: Walking alone while weak and dehydrated risks a fall.
Feeling steady sitting up does not mean the client is safe standing and walking.
Limiting fluids worsens the dehydration the book describes.
Frequent stools with signs of dehydration and weakness raise the risk of falls, so the client needs help with toileting.
questions.clue: Frequent stools with dehydration and weakness.
questions.priority: Prevent falls in a weak, dehydrated client.

questions.stem: A client with ulcerative colitis has been taught about newly prescribed sulfasalazine. Which client statement shows understanding?
options: "This medicine lowers the acid in my stomach."
"This medicine helps control the inflammation in my colon."
"This medicine treats infection in fistulas."
"This medicine replaces nutrients I don't absorb."
rationales: Acid reducers act on the stomach, not the colon.
The book lists sulfasalazine with mesalamine as anti-inflammatory drugs that control inflammation.
Treating infection is the role of antibiotics.
Supplements, not sulfasalazine, replace nutrients.
questions.clue: Sulfasalazine for ulcerative colitis.
questions.priority: Explain the purpose of anti-inflammatory drugs in ulcerative colitis.

questions.stem: A client with diverticulosis calls the clinic with several concerns. Which report should the nurse escalate promptly?
options: Bright red rectal bleeding
Occasional constipation managed with a stool softener
Mild left lower quadrant cramping relieved by passing gas
Wanting more high-fiber recipe ideas
rationales: New rectal bleeding requires prompt triage and assessment of its amount, associated symptoms and hemodynamic status. Endoscopic, interventional-radiology or surgical treatment depends on severity, persistence and localization; bleeding alone does not automatically require surgery.
Stool softeners are part of the treatment for diverticulosis.
LLQ cramping relieved by gas or a bowel movement is a typical finding.
A recipe request is routine teaching.
questions.clue: Rectal bleeding in diverticular disease.
questions.priority: Report bleeding promptly in diverticular disease.

questions.stem: A client recovering from diverticulitis is tolerating liquids. The treating team has prescribed a staged advancement to a low-residue diet before returning to the usual diet. Which diet should the nurse expect next?
options: Regular diet with no restrictions
Return to NPO
High-fiber diet
Low-residue diet
rationales: Incorrect. This client has a specifically prescribed low-residue next stage.
Incorrect. No intolerance or new complication requiring a return to NPO is described.
Incorrect. A high-fiber diet is not the prescribed immediate next stage.
Correct. Follow this individualized order while assessing tolerance; all clients do not require the same fixed dietary sequence.
questions.clue: Tolerating liquids after NPO.
questions.priority: Follow the diet progression after diverticulitis.
questions.takeaway: Advance diet according to clinical improvement, tolerance and the individualized order; NPO and fixed stages are not universal.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client with diverticular disease. For each finding, indicate whether it is consistent with diverticular disease.
rows: Left lower quadrant cramping relieved by gas or a bowel movement
Pain at McBurney point
Rectal bleeding
Abdominal mass with distention
Pain radiating to the right scapula
rationales: LLQ cramping relieved by gas or a bowel movement is a listed finding.
McBurney point tenderness is a sign of appendicitis.
Rectal bleeding is a listed symptom.
An abdominal mass and distention are listed exam findings.
Pain radiating to the right scapula suggests gallbladder disease.
questions.clue: Left-sided findings of diverticular disease.
questions.priority: Recognize the assessment findings of diverticular disease.

questions.stem: A client with diverticular disease says flare-ups seem to come during stressful weeks and that worrying about the next flare is wearing them down. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
options: Explore the client's stressors and teach stress-reduction strategies.
Recommend a low-fiber diet during stressful weeks.
Tell the client that stress has no effect on bowel symptoms.
Advise the client to avoid social activities.
rationales: The book says symptoms can be aggravated by stress and lists stress reduction as nursing support.
The book teaches a high-fiber diet to prevent problems.
The book says stress can aggravate symptoms.
Avoiding social activities does not address stress and may increase isolation.
questions.clue: Symptoms worsen with stress, and the client is worn down.
questions.priority: Support coping with stress-reduction strategies.

questions.stem: The nurse is caring for four clients admitted with diverticulitis. Which client is at greatest risk for a severe course and needs the closest monitoring?
options: A client who followed a high-fiber diet before admission
A client whose pain is easing on IV fluids and bowel rest
A client with a first episode and mild LLQ tenderness
A client taking immunosuppressants after a kidney transplant
rationales: A high-fiber diet is protective, not a risk factor.
Improving pain suggests the treatment is working.
A mild first episode carries less risk than immunocompromise.
The book says recurrence and severity are higher in immunocompromised clients.
questions.clue: Immunocompromise in diverticulitis.
questions.priority: Prioritize monitoring for clients at highest risk of complications.

questions.stem: An adult with complicated diverticulitis and systemic infection is receiving a prescribed antimicrobial regimen of ceftriaxone plus metronidazole. Which medication actions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
options: Give a stimulant laxative to relieve the acute inflammation
Administer prescribed metronidazole for anaerobic coverage
Start an anticholinergic routinely without a separate indication
Start a fiber supplement despite acute intolerance
Administer prescribed ceftriaxone for additional enteric bacterial coverage
rationales: Incorrect. A laxative does not treat the infection and may be inappropriate with the complication.
Correct. Metronidazole supplies anaerobic coverage in this defined regimen.
Incorrect. Routine anticholinergic therapy is not established and requires a specific indication and contraindication review.
Incorrect. Acute diet and supplements depend on tolerance and the treatment plan.
Correct. Ceftriaxone complements anaerobic coverage in the prescribed regimen; selection depends on illness severity and local resistance.
questions.clue: Drugs listed for diverticulitis.
questions.priority: Anticipate drug therapy for diverticulitis.
questions.takeaway: Antibiotics are indicated in this complicated presentation; mild uncomplicated disease may be managed selectively without antibiotics.

questions.stem: A client with recurrent diverticulitis is scheduled for an elective bowel resection and may need an ostomy. Which action best supports continuity of care at discharge?
options: Arrange wound and ostomy care teaching and support before discharge.
Ask assistive personnel to teach ostomy care.
Give the client a pamphlet with no follow-up plan.
Wait until the first clinic visit to discuss ostomy care.
rationales: The book lists elective resection after recurrent episodes and wound/ostomy care support as nursing care.
Teaching is not delegated to assistive personnel.
A pamphlet alone does not provide the support the client needs.
Waiting leaves the client unprepared at home.
questions.clue: Planned resection with a possible ostomy.
questions.priority: Plan discharge support for wound and ostomy care.

questions.stem: A client with right lower quadrant pain has a CT scan. Which finding supports appendicitis?
options: An enlarged, thick-walled appendix
Gallbladder wall thickening with fluid around it
An enlarged pancreas with fluid collections
Diverticula with wall thickening in the sigmoid colon
rationales: The book says CT shows an enlarged, thick-walled appendix.
Gallbladder wall thickening suggests cholecystitis.
An enlarged pancreas with fluid suggests pancreatitis.
Sigmoid diverticula suggest diverticular disease.
questions.clue: CT for RLQ pain.
questions.priority: Interpret imaging in suspected appendicitis.

questions.stem: A client diagnosed with appendicitis says, "Surgery scares me more than this pain. Can't I just wait and see if it goes away?" Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "There's nothing to be afraid of. Just sign the form."
"You don't have a choice. The surgery is already scheduled."
"Your fear makes sense. Delaying care can lead to rupture. What worries you most?"
"Waiting is fine; appendicitis usually settles on its own."
rationales: This minimizes the client's fear.
This dismisses the client's right to make an informed decision.

The book says complications such as rupture, peritonitis and sepsis cause most deaths, not the surgery itself; acknowledging the fear, giving accurate information and exploring concerns supports an informed choice.
Appendicitis can progress to rupture, so this is false reassurance.
questions.clue: Fear of surgery leading to a wish to delay.
questions.priority: Address fear while giving accurate information about risk.

questions.stem: A client with appendicitis is awaiting surgery. Which findings suggest rupture and must be reported immediately? Select all that apply.
options: A sudden decrease in pain followed by diffuse abdominal pain
Pain that stays localized at McBurney point
A rigid, board-like abdomen
A rising WBC with a left shift
Falling blood pressure
Lying still with the right knee flexed
rationales: The book lists a sudden decrease in pain, then increasing diffuse pain, as a rupture sign.
Localized McBurney point tenderness is a classic appendicitis sign, not a rupture sign.
A rigid, board-like abdomen is a listed rupture sign.
A rising WBC with left shift is a listed rupture sign.
Falling blood pressure is a late rupture sign.
Lying still with the right knee flexed is a typical appendicitis observation.
questions.clue: Signs listed for suspected rupture.
questions.priority: Recognize and report signs of appendix rupture.

questions.stem: A client with acute appendicitis has several orders. For each one, indicate its purpose.
rows: Lactated Ringer's
Cefotetan
Morphine
Metronidazole
rationales: The book lists NS or LR to replace fluid losses.
Cefotetan is a listed antibiotic.
The book lists morphine as safe for acute abdominal pain.
Metronidazole is a listed antibiotic.
questions.clue: Fluids, antibiotics and analgesics in appendicitis.
questions.priority: Match appendicitis drugs with their purpose.

questions.stem: A client with suspected appendicitis is lying still on the stretcher with the right knee flexed. What should the nurse do?
options: Turn the client prone to relax the abdomen.
Let the client stay in this position of comfort.
Help the client walk to ease the pain.
Ask the client to straighten both legs and lie flat.
rationales: Lying prone puts pressure on the painful abdomen.
The book notes clients prefer to lie still with the right knee flexed; allowing this position promotes comfort.
Walking is not a comfort measure before surgery.
Straightening the legs works against the position the client has chosen for comfort.
questions.clue: Lying still with the right knee flexed.
questions.priority: Support the client's position of comfort.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client the day after appendectomy. For each finding, indicate whether it is expected or should be reported.
rows: Mild incisional pain controlled with analgesics
Rigid abdomen with a new fever
Walking in the hall with assistance
Tolerating a regular diet
Rising heart rate with spreading abdominal pain
rationales: Pain management is part of routine postoperative care.
Rigidity and fever suggest peritonitis, a complication that delays discharge.
Early ambulation is expected.
Diet as tolerated is expected.
A rising heart rate with spreading pain suggests peritonitis.
questions.clue: Signs of peritonitis versus normal recovery.
questions.priority: Identify postoperative complications that need reporting.

questions.stem: A client awaiting appendectomy is NPO under current orders. During an operating-room delay, abdominal pain worsens and the temperature rises to 102.2°F (39°C). Which action best advocates for the client?
options: Apply a heating pad without further assessment
Reassure the client that surgery can wait several more days
Notify the surgical team promptly of the changed findings and reassess the client
Offer oral fluids despite the NPO order
rationales: Incorrect. Heat does not address deterioration and should not replace assessment and escalation.
Incorrect. Worsening findings need evaluation; the nurse cannot guarantee that delay is safe.
Correct. The change may indicate progression or a complication and requires timely surgical reassessment.
Incorrect. Follow the NPO and prescribed IV hydration plan while the surgical team reassesses.
questions.clue: The client is approaching the end of the ideal surgical window.
questions.priority: Advocate for timely surgery.
questions.takeaway: Escalate changing clinical findings and advocate for the individualized surgical plan; do not use a universal symptom-onset cutoff.

concerns.issue: Gastritis is numbered C3, the same as Peptic Ulcer Disease on page 72; later sections (Cirrhosis C4 through Appendicitis C9) leave the chapter with 10 topics but only 9 numbers.
GERD management table: the first row label reads 'Antacids Proton Pump Inhibitors' with '(PPIs)' on the next row, so the antacid and PPI row labels run together.

Metoclopramide (GI stimulant) is given the same purpose as H2 blockers ('Reduce gastric acid production; useful in mild to moderate cases'), which looks copied from the row above; metoclopramide is a prokinetic, not an acid-reducing drug.
Esophageal pH monitoring lists normal as pH > 5 and abnormal as pH < 5; the usual reflux threshold is pH < 4, so this cutoff should be checked.

Normal serum amylase is given as 100-300 units/L and lipase is said to rise within 2 hours; both differ from commonly used references (amylase roughly 30-110 U/L; lipase rises about 4-8 hours after onset) and should be checked.

Avoiding morphine because of sphincter of Oddi spasm is older teaching that is no longer well supported. It also contradicts page 89, which says morphine is safe for acute abdominal pain, while pages 82 and 87 favor meperidine/Demerol.

The Remember box about Turner's sign and Cullen's sign is on a Cirrhosis page; these signs are listed as pancreatitis findings on page 69, so the box looks misplaced. Page 69 also calls it 'Grey Turner sign' while page 79 calls it 'Turner's sign'.
Typo: 'Ca ions bids to citrate' should read 'binds'.
Typo in the History box: 'fa-ttyy foods' should be 'fatty foods'.

'Medical dissolution is rare for nonobese patients with small cholesterol stones and a functional gallbladder' reads backwards; dissolution therapy is usually reserved for exactly those patients. The lab table also has the typo 'obststruction'.
Causes box lists 'meperidine, methylpredsisolone' under associated conditions for appendicitis without explanation; 'methylpredsisolone' is misspelled (methylprednisolone).
The Remember box on colostomy stoma assessment is in the Appendicitis section, but appendectomy does not normally create a colostomy, so it looks misplaced.
The diverticular disease causes text on page 87 repeats the Causes text on page 86 almost word for word.
In-text citation 'Bosch, Gracia-Sancho, & Abrades, 2020' does not match the reference list spelling 'Abraldes' (page 90).
In-text citation 'Barnes et al., 2022' does not match the reference list, which gives Barnes et al. (2020) (page 90).

The reference list has the same Chouairi et al. article twice (2021 advance online and 2022 print). That article is about gallstone pancreatitis cholecystectomy disparities but is cited for general pancreatitis (page 69) and cholecystitis (page 81) background.

Routine NG tube to suction and TPN 'within 3 days if needed' reflect older practice; current acute pancreatitis guidance favors early oral/enteral feeding, with NG suction for ileus or persistent vomiting and parenteral nutrition only if enteral feeding fails. Peritoneal lavage is also rarely used now. No questions were built on these points.
Sandostatin (octreotide) drip is listed for gastritis bleeding; octreotide is mainly used for variceal bleeding, so its place here should be checked. No questions were built on it.

Demerol (meperidine) is called the preferred analgesic for cholecystitis (also page 87 for diverticulitis); meperidine is now generally discouraged because of its neurotoxic metabolite. No questions were built on this.

5-ASA (mesalamine) is called first-line for Crohn disease; current guidelines find limited benefit of mesalamine in Crohn disease (it is first-line for ulcerative colitis). Questions avoid the 'first-line' claim.

In the Medical Management box, outpatient criteria and 'Initial treatment' are given without a source for the 48-hour/72-hour surgical timing; the open cholecystectomy 'within 72 hours' window should be checked.

The gastritis 'Pharmacologic Highlights' table (PPI, vasopressor, antibiotics, antacids, bismuth, vitamin B12) is printed on page 78, which falls in the Cirrhosis section's page range, so gastritis questions cannot link to it; the table may belong on page 77.
Urine output < 1 mL/kg/hr is given as the hypoperfusion signal; the threshold commonly used is < 0.5 mL/kg/hr, so this number should be checked. No v3 questions use it.
The Cirrhosis - Assessment History box is cut off at the bottom of the panel (text after 'Bleeding: Easy bruising, nosebleeds, bleeding gums' is clipped).

Nursing Care says 'Avoid strain: no heavy lifting, coughing'; advising clients to avoid coughing is unusual and may need rewording (e.g., splint when coughing). No v3 questions use the coughing advice.

"Cystic fibrosis is the leading cause in children" overstates current data; pediatric acute pancreatitis is most often biliary, drug-related, traumatic, systemic or idiopathic, while CFTR and other genetic causes lead in recurrent/chronic disease. A v3 item built on this was rewritten.

H. pylori serum IgG antibody testing is listed as an H. pylori test (also p76). Current guidelines advise against serology because it cannot tell active from past infection; urea breath, stool antigen or biopsy-based tests are preferred. Triple therapy with clarithromycin is also no longer the preferred first-line regimen in many regions.
"Malnutrition, protein deficiency" is listed as a cause of cirrhosis; this is not a recognized independent cause by current standards and should be checked.

Albumin is given as an example of IV fluid resuscitation alongside lactated Ringer's; current guidance favors goal-directed crystalloid (LR) and does not support routine albumin. Dopamine as the vasopressor is also older practice (norepinephrine is usually preferred).
Vasopressin infusion to stop gastritis bleeding (also p78 table) is older practice; current management relies on PPIs, endoscopic therapy and transfusion. Items only test its purpose.
